summary.text: The arrow of time is the idea that time has one direction, so the past and the future are clearly different.
At the microscopic level physical laws look much the same run forwards or backwards, yet everyday events such as a bouncing ball coming to rest do not run in reverse.
Arthur Eddington developed the idea in 1927, tying the direction of time to growing randomness, and it is still an unsolved question in physics.

facts.label: The video test
facts.value: Time-symmetric events look real forwards or backwards

facts.label: Carroll's view
facts.value: Arrows come from our nearness in time to the Big Bang

items.prompt: You watch two clips played in reverse. In one a ball is tossed up and falls back. In the other a ball bounces lower each time until it rests. Which looks wrong in reverse?

options.label: The tossed ball, since it falls on its own
Neither; both run equally well in reverse
Both, since balls cannot move upward alone
The bouncing ball that comes to rest

items.explain: The toss is time-reversible, but a ball bouncing to a stop is not: kinetic energy is dissipated and entropy increases.

items.prompt: A ball resting on the floor never starts bouncing by itself and rises higher each time. What explains this?

options.label: Bouncing needs entropy to go down, which does not happen
Gravity only pulls in one direction
The floor absorbs the ball's weight
Balls lose their mass when they stop

items.explain: Bouncing to a stop dissipates kinetic energy and raises entropy, which is why the process is not time-reversible; gravity itself is reversible.

items.prompt: Following Eddington, you compare two snapshots of the same gas. The second shows more of the random element in the state of the world. Which way along time does the arrow point?

options.label: From the second snapshot toward the first
From the first snapshot toward the second
It cannot be told from randomness
Both directions equally

items.explain: If following the arrow shows more and more randomness, it points toward the future.

items.prompt: You remember yesterday's lunch but not tomorrow's. According to the causal arrow of time, why?

options.label: Future events are too complicated to store
Our brains are built to ignore the future
Past events cause our present memories; future ones do not
Time moves faster toward the future

items.explain: Past events, but not future events, are the cause of present memories, as correlations form between the outer world and our brain.

items.prompt: Physical laws mostly do not care which way is up, yet near Earth up and down feel very different. What does Sean Carroll draw from this about time?

options.label: Time's direction may come from our nearness to the Big Bang
Time has a built-in direction in every law of physics
Space and time are really the same thing
Gravity is the cause of time's direction

items.explain: Carroll compares it to Earth breaking up-down symmetry: laws are largely time-symmetric, but near the Big Bang there is an obvious forward and backward.

items.prompt: English speakers talk about looking forward to the future and looking back on the past. What does this show?

options.label: That the future is physically ahead of us in space
That all languages agree on time's direction
That physics proves time moves in front of us
That linking behind with past is culturally determined

items.explain: The association of behind with past and ahead with future is culturally determined, not a physical fact.
